title: VC0-01868
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) is a citizen of Haiti, and his minor daughters XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of the United States of America (U.S.). The Principal Appellant is the designated representative of the minor Appellants.

The claim of the Appellants' spouse/mother was joined to those of the Appellants, and the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that she established a nexus to membership in a particular social group and that she would face more than a mere possibility of gender-based persecution.

The Principal Appellant fears criminals in Haiti will target him due to a perception that he is wealthy. The RPD found the Principal Appellant did not establish a nexus to a Convention ground, identified credibility issues and concluded that the Principal Appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence that he is personally at risk in Haiti. The RPD also found that the minor Appellants did not make any allegations against the U.S.

The Appellants identify several issues with the RPD decision. The Appellants submit new evidence under section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and seek a hearing pursuant to section 110(6). I have accepted some of the new evidence but deny their request for a hearing.

Following my own review, I find that the Principal Appellant did not establish that he faces a prospective risk in Haiti or that the minor Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution or risk in the US.

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. NEW EVIDENCE Some the evidence presented by the Appellants is accepted

The Appellants' claims were heard on February 17, 2020, and the RPD gave its decision on February 24, 2020. The Appellants presented new evidence with the perfection of their appeal on September 25, 2020.

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that an appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. In Singh,1 the Federal Court of Appeal dictates a narrow interpretation of section 110(4): the conditions set out therein must be met, and there is no room for discretion on the part of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) . If the section 110(4) threshold is met, then the new evidence must also meet jurisprudential requirements of credibility, relevance and newness.2

The Appellants presented the following new evidence with the perfection of their appeal: A. Letter dated "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX" from the Principal Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX;3 B. Letter undated from the Principal Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX;4 C. Letter dated Tuesday, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, from the Principal Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX;5 D. Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, Haiti: Treatment by society of Haitians who have lived for a long time abroad, especially in Canada, after they return to their country; whether they are at risk of being victims of violence, and including the type of violence and from whom; whether their return could represent a threat to their families (2018-August 2020), HTI200334.FE, 27 August 2020;6 E. JosÚ Miguel Vivanco, Concerns Raised Over Planned Gang Raid in Haiti, Human Rights Watch, April 28, 2020;7 F. Unattributed, The bandits control the territory": resurgence of armed violence in Haiti, France Media Agency, August 5, 2020;8 G. Jacqueline Charles, Criminal gangs for hire: Corrupt cops and the fight for votes in Haiti's next elections, Miami Herald, June 26, 2020;9 H. Unattributed, Haiti - Insecurity : 616 victims of homicides in 5 months, Haiti Libre, June 23, 2020;10 I. Haiti 2020 Crime & Safety Report, Overseas Security Advisory Council, Bureau of Diplomatic Security, U.S. Department of State, April 29, 2020;11 J. Unattributed, US Urges Citizens to Stay Away From Haiti, PRIDE, March 6, 2020.12

The RAD Rules are very clear that the appellant's memorandum must include full and detailed submissions regarding how any new evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4).13 The Appellants did not make any submissions about the new evidence.

Documents A, B and C are typewritten letters from friends of the Principal Appellant. Document A does not specify the year in the date, document B is not dated at all and none of documents A, B or C are signed. There is no indication how these letters were received by the Appellants and no documents to confirm the identity of the authors are provided. I do not find that documents A, B and C are credible on their face and, therefore, are not admissible as new evidence.

Documents D-J were produced after the RPD decision, so they meet the temporal threshold of section 110(4). Documents D14 and I15 are found in the current version of the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Haiti. Documents E, F, G, H and J are new, published by credible news sources and are relevant to the appeal as an update to country conditions. I find that documents D-J are admissible as new evidence.

The Appellants request that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) hold a hearing. Section 110(6) of the IRPA says the RAD may only hold a hearing if there is new evidence that (a) raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, (b) is central to the RPD's decision, and (c) if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. Since the new evidence I accepted relates to country conditions and does not raise an issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, it does not meet the 110(6) criteria. The hearing request is denied.

The RAD reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing and weighing the oral testimony heard, which in particular cases attracts deference.16 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied the correctness standard.
The determinative issue is whether the RPD was correct in finding that the Principal Appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence that he is personally at risk if he returns to Haiti.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in: making its decision in a perverse or capricious manner without regard to the evidence presented; failing to analyze evidence which corroborated the personal risk of the Principal Appellant as a wealthy returnee; and failing to assess and consider the evidence and provide a forward-looking assessment of risk.

The Appellants do not make any arguments about the RPD finding that the minor Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution or risk in the U.S. and I see no reason to disturb the RPD finding.

Following my review of the record, the testimony, the Appellants' arguments and new evidence, I agree that the RPD did not undertake a fulsome analysis of the Principal Appellant's prospective risk, so I have done so. I find that the Appellants did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they face a prospective risk to their lives or to cruel and unusual punishment in Haiti. Evidence

The Principal Appellant originally testified that he was afraid of "the gang" who attacked his home on XXXX XXXX, 2018, who were "not people that [he] knew."17 When the RPD asked why he thought he was attacked, the Principal Appellant answered, "Well, I don't know the reason."18 When his counsel asked him later in the hearing, the Principal Appellant said that "because for some reason they believe that I am rich."19

The Principal Appellant testified that his problems in Haiti started in XXXX 2018 and he presented the evidence about the following incidents: Date Target Event BOC Testimony Other XXXX and XXXX 2018 Principal Appellant Anonymous telephone death threats to Principal Appellant "I received some messages and anonymous phone calls from my work wanting me to do corruption"20 Certificat de plainte, Le XXXX XXXX 201821 XXXX XXXX, 2018 Principal Appellant and spouse Attack by unidentified armed and masked individuals who fired on their car "XXXX 2018, we were mistreated by a mask person...he fired two gun shot on my vehicle"22 Spouse's statement23 Certificat de plainte Le XXXX XXXX 201824 XXXX XXXX, 2018 Appellants' residence Intrusion, damage and robbery by armed unidentified individuals XXXX 2018 house was attacked by gang of armed people, broke the gate and the front of the house, stole a lot of stuff and killed dogs25 "...on XXXX XXXX, 2018 ...gangsters entered my house and they were shooting and they said that they would rape and kill my family"26 Spouse's statement27 Certificat de plainte Le XXXX XXXX 201828 XXXX XXXX, 2018 Principal Appellant's father-in-law's bag Two armed and unidentified bandits stole bag DÚclaration de perte29 XXXX XXXX, 2019 Principal Appellant's father-in-law's business Fire which started at a neighbour's burnt construction materials Extrait des minutes du Greffe30 XXXX XXXX, 2019 Principal Appellant's mother Victim of physical aggression ...when they attacked my mom they said if they found me they would kill me because I left and they are still looking for me.31 ProcÞs-verbal du XXXX XXXX 201932 Certificat mÚdical33

The Principal Appellant's BOC said that all the Appellants and their spouse/mother travelled to Canada the day after the attack on their home.34 He testified that the family came to Canada because of the XXXX XXXX, 2018, attack,35 and that he returned to Haiti and came back to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018.36 When the RPD asked the Principal Appellant if he made an asylum claim in XXXX, he said, "No, I didn't do that yet because I was somewhat under pressure so much. I was not sure exactly what am I going to do next."37 The Principal Appellant testified that he travelled a lot prior to leaving Haiti and had visited Mexico City, the Dominican Republic, the U.S. and Canada. He said that he visited the U.S. five times.38 RPD findings

Based on the Principal Appellant's evidence that he was targeted by criminals due to their perception of his wealth, the RPD found that he did not establish a nexus to a Convention ground and his claim fails under section 96. The Appellants do not make submissions about this finding and I find that the RPD did not err.

The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's "failure to make an asylum claim in Canada and re-availment to Haiti undermines his credibility regarding how serious he took these attacks and whether or not these are personalized attacks or whether he was a victim of random crime due to the perception that he is wealthy. Given this credibility issue, the panel finds that the [Principal Appellant] has not provided sufficient credible evidence that he is personally at risk if he returns to Haiti."39 Mindful of objective evidence40 indicating that crime, including by various gangs, throughout Haiti is increasing, the RPD restated its finding that the Principal Appellant did not establish that he faces a personal risk if he returns to Haiti. Appellants' arguments

The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in: making its decision in a perverse or capricious manner without regard to the evidence presented; failing to analyze evidence which corroborated the personal risk of the Principal Appellant as a wealthy returnee; and failing to assess and consider the evidence and provide a forward-looking assessment of risk. The Appellants make a number of arguments to support their submissions. Positive determination for co-claimant

The Appellants argue that the RPD's positive determination of the refugee claim of the Principal Appellant's spouse was highly probative and corroborated his allegations. I do not agree, The RPD made its positive determination based on the Principal Appellant's spouse's membership in a particular social group and that she would face more than a mere possibility of gender-based persecution. Credibility

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred as it simply searched through the Principal Appellant's testimony, looking for inconsistencies or evidence that lacks credibility in order to build a case against his credibility. I do not agree. The RPD based its credibility finding on the Principal Appellant's failure to claim refugee protection after the XXXX XXXX, 2018, attack and his re-availment to Haiti.

The Appellants argue that the RPD unreasonably rejected the Principal Appellant's explanation for his return to Haiti which was corroborated by his spouse and employer. The Appellants argue that the Principal Appellant "testified that due to safety of his life his employer, XXXX XXXX transferred him to another place, department XXXX, where he was traced and had threats from bandits who started following him demanding money he carried from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX employees wages and fearing risk to his life he resigned and fled Haiti on XXXX XXXX, 2018, and claimed protection of Canada."41
I agree with the Appellants that the RPD did not reference the explanation for the Principal Appellant's return to Haiti, so I will consider that evidence.

I have reviewed the transcript of the RPD hearing and note that neither the Principal Appellant nor his spouse gave any testimony about why the Principal Appellant returned to Haiti; however, their counsel did make detailed submissions.42 The Principal Appellant's BOC says, "I went back home, I think I could work in a different place but it was not a success. I continued to receive attack from different people." His spouse's statement makes the Appellants' argument referenced above almost verbatim.43

The evidence from the Principal Appellant's employer is mixed. One letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, not on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX letterhead, references a transfer to XXXX but does not give any dates and makes no reference to the Principal Appellant's being traced and threatened in XXXX. Another letter on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX letterhead dated XXXX XXXX, 2018,44 makes no reference to any transfer and the Principal Appellant's XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX identity card, valid until XXXX XXXX, 2018, says that he is based in Port-au-Prince.45 I also note that the Principal Appellant's immigration form which he signed on XXXX XXXX, 2018, says that he worked in Port-au-Prince from XXXX 2017 to XXXX 2018.

I find that the evidence which would corroborate the Principal Appellant's explanation for returning to Haiti in July 2018 is inconsistent and contradictory, which adversely impacts the credibility of his explanation. Prospective risk

The Appellants submit that the RPD erred as it failed to acknowledge and assess crucial documentary evidence in its section 97 analysis of the prospective personal risk of the Principal Appellant as a wealthy returnee. I agree that the RPD did not undertake a fulsome prospective risk analysis or reference the Appellants documentary evidence, so I have done so.

A determination of whether the Principal Appellant is a person in need of protection involves an analysis of the nature of the risk at issue, of the likelihood that the Principal Appellant would be subject to that risk, and, if so, whether the same risk is faced generally by others.

The Federal Court46 recently summarized the two-part test applicable to a section 97 analysis: First, the RPD should consider whether there is an ongoing future risk, and if so, what precisely the risk is. Once this is done, the RPD must next compare the risk faced by the claimant to that faced by a significant group in the country of nationality to determine whether the risks are of the same nature and degree. If the risks are not the same, the claimant will be entitled to protection under section 97. See Portillo at paras 40-41. As Justice Gleason later explained in Ortega [citation omitted], the second step in the inquiry "is a forward-looking inquiry and is concerned not so much with the cause of the risk but rather with the likelihood of what will happen to the claimant in the future as compared to all or a significant segment of the general population" (at para 14).47

The first step is to identify the nature of the risk faced by the Principal Appellant: First, the RPD must correctly characterize the nature of the risk faced by the claimant. This requires the Board to consider whether there is an ongoing future risk, and if so, whether the risk is one of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment. Most importantly, the Board must determine what precisely the risk is.48

I find that the Principal Appellant has not established that he was personally targeted in the XXXX and XXXX 2018 incidents. The evidence is that he did not know and could not identify any of the attackers in any of the incidents. There was no evidence presented to suggest that the two incidents faced by the Principal Appellant's father-in-law in 2018 and 2019 had anything to do with the Principal Appellant. In fact, the evidence presented says that the fire that destroyed the merchandise of his father-in-law in 2019 started on a neighbouring property. The Principal Appellant testified that "people on motorcycles that they don't recognize" attacked his mother in XXXX 2019 and "said if they had found me they would kill me because I left and they are still looking for me."49 This testimony, however, embellishes the police report filed by his mother.50 There is nothing in the evidence which demonstrated that it was the same "unidentified" criminals who were involved in each of the incidents.

I find that the nature of the risk faced by the Principal Appellant is that of random criminal acts by unidentified perpetrators who possibly perceive him to be wealthy and it is an ongoing future risk in Haiti.
The next step is to compare the risk faced by the Principal Appellant to that faced by a significant group in Haiti to determine whether the risks are of the same nature and degree.

Making a general reference to the documentary and new evidence, the Appellants submit that "if they return to Haiti they will face serious threats, robbed, kidnapped and killed as they are considered wealthy and subjected to cruelty, torture and risk of life."51

The objective evidence says that criminality is pervasive in Haiti and affects a large segment of the population and appears to be indiscriminate, affecting rich and poor alike.52 The new evidence presented by the Appellants confirms "an upsurge in violence caused by armed gangs"53 especially in the slums and impoverished neighbourhoods of Haiti.54

The Appellants' new evidence, document D,55 an Immigration and Refugee Board Response to Information Request (2020 RIR)56 is mixed. It says that Haitians returning to Haiti after a long stay abroad risk being targeted by criminals because they are considered to be wealthy, and that young returnees are more frequent targets of criminals than senior citizens who are treated with a measure of respect and compassion.57

The 2020 RIR says that risks a returnee will face depend on the following factors: whether or not the individual fled the community because of political violence; was the witness of a crime; has been accused of a crime; incurred loans that they will not be able to repay; and was caught up in communal violence and has allegiance to a faction.58

The 2020 RIR also says the risk of kidnapping for ransom, for example, is indiscriminate and widespread; members of the general Haitian population, regardless of their rank or social class, are at risk of being kidnapped and everyone is at risk.59

The evidence is that all Haitians, rich and poor, are at risk of being targeted by bandits and gangs. The Principal Appellant has not lived in Canada for a long time, is approaching 40 years old and is not in the high-risk categories identified in the 2020 RIR. I find that the Principal Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that his personal situation would subject him to a risk any different from that faced by most of the Haitian population.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
